name: Florence, Venice, Rome: Cities of the Renaissance
description: Rival city-states in Italy paid for the painters, builders and thinkers who changed European art, and the cities themselves became the great works.

checkpoints.name: Old cities, new voices
checkpoints.note: Venice grew from a lagoon refuge into a sea power ruled by a doge, and its merchants, among them Marco Polo, travelled far to the east. In Florence, Giotto and Dante gave art and poetry fresh directions.

checkpoints.name: Bankers and builders
checkpoints.note: The House of Medici made a fortune through the Medici Bank and ruled Florence from behind the scenes. Their wealth paid for Filippo Brunelleschi and Donatello, while Renaissance humanism revived the study of classical writers.

checkpoints.name: The golden decades
checkpoints.note: Botticelli painted The Birth of Venus, and Leonardo da Vinci painted The Last Supper in Milan. In Florence Michelangelo carved David, and in Rome he painted the Sistine Chapel ceiling while Raphael painted The School of Athens for the popes.

checkpoints.name: Thinkers and trouble
checkpoints.note: Machiavelli wrote about power and politics. Titian painted in Venice, and Galileo Galilei observed the heavens, but in 1633 he was tried by the Church in the Galileo affair. Claudio Monteverdi helped to create opera.

checkpoints.name: Music and the fall of Venice
checkpoints.note: Antonio Vivaldi wrote The Four Seasons in Venice, a city of festivals and carnival. In 1797 the Republic of Venice, which had lasted for more than a thousand years, ended when Napoleon's army arrived.
